writing.explanation:
For [3,9,20,null,null,15,7], leaf heights are 1 and both root subtrees differ by at most one. In [1,2,null,3], root subtree heights differ by 2, so the sentinel reaches the root and returns false.

The worked program is a complete executable for this pattern. Its core function uses typed input so the state transitions remain visible. The challenge input contract is: Parse the compact level-order binary tree, where null omits a node. Return true exactly when every subtree has child heights differing by at most one. The visible fixture is `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]` and its example result is `true`. The implementation and additional semantic fixtures were checked against an independent reference calculation. Those bounded tests establish these examples; they are not a proof for all inputs or a measurement on an iPhone.

Return a canonical String from solve: lowercase true/false for booleans; decimal integers without extra signs, leading zeros or whitespace; comma-separated sequence values and semicolon-separated groups. Whole-number medians have no decimal suffix; half medians use .5. Do not append a newline to the returned value. Preserve the explicitly named textual sentinels such as none or #. Input fixtures are bounded so the demonstrated arithmetic fits its named Rust types; satisfy the stated input preconditions before applying the algorithm.

String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

A problem is a good match for Height with Balance Sentinel when it asks for balanced-tree validation without repeated heights. Here the concrete task is: Parse the compact level-order binary tree, where null omits a node. Return true exactly when every subtree has child heights differing by at most one. The visible input `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]` is an example, not a definition of the whole problem. Ask what operations the solution must support and what the input guarantees. Look for hierarchy and parent-child structure; a plain sequence algorithm loses the branching relationships. The right choice follows from those guarantees, not from a familiar noun in the prompt.

The decisive invariant is: Return height normally but propagate a sentinel immediately when a subtree is already unbalanced. Try to say why it applies to the task without quoting the implementation. Which fact becomes known after one update, and which possible answers remain? A tree result is built from a node and its children. Decide whether information flows downward, upward, or in level order. If that claim cannot be maintained on a legal input, the pattern is wrong or one of its preconditions is missing. A counterexample is more useful than a vague warning: change one property of the sample, trace the first two steps, and identify the exact claim that fails.

Compare costs before committing. The advertised bound is O(n) time · O(h) stack; identify the operation responsible for it and the extra memory it needs. Then compare a straightforward alternative: a direct scan, full sort, or repeated recomputation may be easier but can pay for the same work many times. Do not choose the more elaborate method just because it has a famous name. For the sample, predict `true` and explain which part of the state lets the method reach that result.

When the prompt is ambiguous, ask about input size, ordering, duplicates, and required output format. Test a missing root, a leaf, a skewed tree, and equal or duplicate values when ordering rules depend on them. Use references for read-only traversals and make the stack or queue explicit when recursion depth might be large. The Rust sketch can show a useful primitive without proving that the whole task is solved; connect each primitive to the requested output. You should be able to name a fitting case, a near miss, and the assumption separating them before writing the first line.
